analysis.one_liner: Bans mining on Oak Flat, a sacred Western Apache site in Arizona's Tonto National Forest.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 23 Democratic cosponsors, has sat in the House Natural Resources Committee since March 2026 with no hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would permanently withdraw the Chí'chil Biłdagoteel (Oak Flat) Historic District — thousands of acres of Tonto National Forest listed on the National Register of Historic Places as a sacred Western Apache site — from all mining, mineral leasing, and mining-related construction like pipelines, power lines, and roads. It directs the Forest Service to preserve the land's natural condition and consult with tribes on access for traditional ceremonies. This blocks the Resolution Copper mine, a joint venture of the foreign mining giants Rio Tinto and BHP, whose project would collapse the surface into a mile-wide crater and drain local groundwater.
analysis.who_benefits: Western Apache tribes whose ancestors were removed from the area in the 1880s and who still hold ceremonies, gather foods and medicines, and bury their dead there; regional Arizona communities whose groundwater and springs would otherwise be drawn down by the mine; and downstream communities who would otherwise face a 1.37-billion-ton toxic waste dump in the Gila River watershed.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Western Apache tribes and Arizona communities

how_it_helps.text: The bill withdraws all National Forest System land in the Chí'chil Biłdagoteel Historic District from entry under the mining laws and from mineral and geothermal leasing, prohibiting mining and mining-related infrastructure such as waste pipelines, power lines, and roads on the land.

It directs the Secretary of Agriculture to preserve the natural condition of the land, prohibit activities harming its landscape, water, and wildlife, and consult government-to-government with tribes with ties to the site, entering cooperative agreements to guarantee access for traditional activities.

The bill's findings document that the Forest Service's own studies identified the site as sacred to Western Apaches and important to at least nine tribes, with hundreds of cultural resources and 46 culturally important springs, and that the mine would consume over 250 billion gallons of groundwater and create a crater 1.8 miles wide and 1,000 feet deep.

analysis.who_pays: Resolution Copper — a joint venture of Rio Tinto (55%) and BHP (45%) — would lose its ability to build the mine and its supporting infrastructure on federal land in the historic district, and copper supply from the deposit would never be developed.
analysis.who_pays_short: The Rio Tinto–BHP copper joint venture

drawbacks.text: The bill cannot undo the transfer that already happened: by the time it was introduced, roughly 2,422 acres of the district had already been conveyed to Resolution Copper under the 2014 land exchange, and the bill's withdrawal applies only to land still in the National Forest System.

Copper is essential to electrification and manufacturing, and blocking a major domestic copper deposit means that demand must be met elsewhere; the bill's own findings concede that the mine's copper was never required to be sold or used in the United States, but critics of the mine's opponents generally argue the country needs the metal.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is permanent protection of a registered historic and sacred site, tribal religious freedom, and regional groundwater, against the cost of leaving a large copper deposit in the ground. The bill's own findings note the copper was slated primarily for export and that no law required it to benefit U.S. consumers, which weakens the national-supply argument for the mine. The main design weakness is that the bill comes after the core parcel was already handed over, so it protects the surrounding federal land and blocks mine infrastructure there but cannot restore the land itself.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Natural Resources Committee, which has taken no action on it so far.

narrative.text: Rep. Adelita Grijalva introduced the bill on March 17, 2026, joined by Reps. Stansbury, Leger Fernandez, and Huffman, and 23 House Democrats had signed on as cosponsors.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources, and the action history shows no hearing, markup, or vote since.

The bill responds to a 2014 land-exchange rider that gave Resolution Copper roughly 2,422 acres within the historic district, a transfer the bill's definitions say was completed on or about March 13, 2026, days before the bill was introduced.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has either gained or lost — the bill is simply sitting in committee, and the mine transfer has proceeded while the protective legislation waits.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: So far, nobody — the bill is waiting in committee

for.name: Rep. Adelita S. Grijalva
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to withdraw the Chí'chil Biłdagoteel Historic District from mining and direct the Forest Service to preserve it.

sides.party_line_note: All 24 members attached to the bill — the sponsor and 23 cosponsors — are House Democrats, and no Republican has signed on.

industries.industry: Copper mining (Resolution Copper, a Rio Tinto–BHP joint venture)
industries.note: The bill bans all mining and mine infrastructure on the federal land in the historic district, blocking the project. The company has already received title to 2,422 acres through the 2014 land exchange, so the bill protects the remaining public land but cannot touch the parcel already conveyed.

industries.industry: Foreign mining conglomerates (Rio Tinto and BHP)
industries.note: The bill's findings describe the mine as serving export markets, primarily China, with no requirement that extracted copper benefit U.S. consumers, while the mine's water use and waste dump would fall on Arizona communities. The companies keep the parcel they already acquired but lose the federal-land infrastructure the mine needs.

analysis.trajectory: Bills that sit in the Natural Resources Committee without a hearing rarely move, and this one faces a Republican-controlled House with no Republican cosponsors; similar Oak Flat protection bills in past Congresses never reached a floor vote. The realistic path is that the bill dies quietly at the end of the 119th Congress unless a committee hearing or a broader public-lands package picks it up.
